source.title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes
source.authors: Leonardo Galli; Curtis Fox; Wiebke Bartolomaeus; Mark Schmidt; Holger Rauhut

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents reading the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how large, adaptively selected gradient steps affect training loss, using line searches and other step-size methods rather than the fixed learning-rate threshold recipe in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss outcomes for its own large-step training experiments. Its classification-accuracy and sharpness findings are not rows for these versions because they do not measure the training classification error or the fixed-rate stability-threshold behavior named in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses edge-of-stability findings to design adaptive step-size algorithms and evaluates their convergence. Its large adaptive steps are not identified relative to the initial linearized-model stability limit, and its changing learning rates do not test the fixed-rate sharpening and stability-threshold dynamics in V5. Appendix D also changes learning rates during warmup without establishing that initial threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially correct. More precisely, the authors define large steps and develop first-order algorithms to select them, report edge-of-stability behavior, and find that early encounters with globally flat saddles can severely slow optimization. For the tested MSE classification experiments, capping NLS step sizes below the number of classes avoids these regions and often improves training loss and test accuracy; they call for larger experiments to confirm the performance conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses full-batch GD with adaptive nonmonotone equality line searches and compares them with other adaptive step-size methods; it does not use the fixed learning-rate-above-initial-stability-limit recipe described in V5.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on the line-search variant and whether the step size is bounded below the number of classes; reaching the globally-flat region early is associated with poor training convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Adaptive nonmonotone line searches can encounter globally flat saddle regions early and stall near constant-output loss. Successful-flat runs approach slightly sharper regions and can attain low loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested adaptive training algorithms, attaining minimal sharpness early can impair convergence; low sharpness alone does not establish successful optimization.

fits_no_version.finding: Bounding NLS step sizes below the number of classes avoids the MSE globally flat regions and often improves training performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An upper bound on adaptive learning rates can improve convergence by preventing early entry into globally flat saddle regions.

fits_no_version.finding: The study measures sharpness together with adaptive learning rates and loss, reporting edge-of-stability behavior from the beginning. Appendix D also reports poorer convergence after warmup to 125 than after warmup capped at 90 on CIFAR100–ResNet34.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive or warmed-up learning-rate schedules can produce stability-related oscillations and flattening, with convergence depending on the schedule.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), as stated in the paper.
record.problems: The main deterministic experiments use subsamples of 5000 images; the authors say larger experiments are needed to confirm the conclusions. Several plotted outcomes have no exact values in the prose. The study does not directly test fixed learning rates against the initial linearized-model stability threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separate numeric training-loss rows extracted from figures because values are shown only as plots and the prose does not specify exact values. See Figures 1, 3, 5–26, and 32–39.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error under SGD or Adam on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels and the stated size, stopping, and regularization conditions. The training-accuracy panels concern adaptive full-batch GD and do not supply this test.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Depth-related training degradation and matched identity-shortcut comparisons, including the stated initialization exceptions.
Effects of activation-matched initialization, orthogonality, and convolution kernels on training speed and trainable depth.
Recovery and divergence relative to the initial linearized-model stability limit; fixed-rate progressive sharpening and sustained threshold tracking; divergence despite starting below that threshold.
Matched batch-normalization interventions on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, or a Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: All five corrected states concern whether the rows establish a claim-version effect; they do not dispute the explicitly reported loss stagnation. Adaptive learning rates above a contemporaneous threshold cannot by themselves establish V5's initial-threshold recovery or fixed-rate dynamics. Additional plotted loss outcomes are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training classification error, corrupted or random labels, or comparisons varying model size and early stopping.
Does not study two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks or spurious local minima.
Does not compare plain and residual networks as a test of depth-related training error; batch normalization is removed in the reported ResNet experiments.
Uses PyTorch default initialization but does not compare initialization methods or test training speed across depth.
Does not test fixed learning rates against the initial linearized-model stability limit, or map the divergence threshold described in V5.
Does not test batch normalization as a training-speed or learning-rate-tolerance intervention.

rows.subject: CNN on EMNIST letters
rows.size_stated: CNN: convolutional layers with 32 output channels; linear layer input dimension 2048; 26 classes
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch GD with PoNLS line search and MSE loss
rows.value: The method is stuck at the same training loss throughout all of training.
rows.note: Authors explicitly describe the loss as unchanged throughout training; this is a failure to reduce training loss, not a reported training classification error.
rows.check: The unchanged loss is explicitly reported, but it measures PoNLS convergence rather than recovery above V5's specified stability limit. It cannot establish an absent V5 effect.

rows.subject: resnet34
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch GD with NLS line search and MSE loss
rows.value: When the globally-flat region is encountered early, the loss does not decrease below the random-guessing value; for K=10, the text gives 0.09.
rows.note: The paper describes poor training convergence when the globally-flat region is reached early; the stated 0.09 is the random-guessing loss reference, not a measured final value for this specific model.
rows.check: The stalled NLS run does not test V5's learning-rate conditions. The 0.09 value is a calculated constant-output baseline, not an exact measured final loss. ResNet34 has batch normalization removed.

rows.subject: resnet34
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch GD with NLS-ub line search and MSE loss
rows.value: Training performance is often better than CDAT; no exact training-loss value stated.
rows.note: The text does not give an exact loss value for this setting.
rows.check: This is the proposed method's performance comparison with CDAT, not a measurement of V5. The general statement that NLS-ub often performs better does not establish this particular run's comparative outcome. ResNet34 has batch normalization removed.

rows.subject: vgg11
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch GD with NLS line search and MSE loss
rows.value: Successful-flat runs often achieve very low training loss; exact value not stated.
rows.note: The paper classifies CIFAR100×vgg11 as successfully-flat, with sharpness slightly above 2/K; no exact training-loss value is provided in the prose.
rows.check: Low loss under adaptive NLS does not establish recovery from a learning rate above the initial stability limit or fixed-rate edge-of-stability dynamics. The general successful-flat description supplies no exact final loss for this run.

rows.subject: vgg11
rows.operation_detail: Full-batch GD with NLS-ub line search and MSE loss
rows.value: Training performance is often better than CDAT; no exact training-loss value stated.
rows.note: The authors say NLS-ub often improves training performance relative to CDAT; the text does not provide an exact value for this setting.
rows.check: This is the proposed method's performance comparison with CDAT. The cited general statement does not establish the specific CIFAR100–VGG11 comparison, and neither outcome measures V5.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Large adaptive steps that reach globally-flat regions early in the tested MSE classification runs
reader_labels.reason: Some runs fail to lower training loss beyond the random-guessing reference or remain stuck, while the NLS-ub runs often improve training performance; see R1–R3.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Successful-flat runs in the tested MSE classification experiments
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that successful-flat runs often attain very low training loss; see R4.
